question: Which of the following best describes the fundamental legal distinction between real property and personal property?
choice_a: Real property is land and everything permanently attached to it; personal property is movable and not permanently affixed
choice_b: Real property includes only buildings; personal property includes land
choice_c: Real property can be owned only by corporations; personal property can be owned only by individuals
choice_d: Real property is always taxed; personal property is never taxed
explanation: Real property (realty) consists of land and everything permanently attached to it, including the airspace above and the subsurface below. Personal property (chattel or personalty) is movable property not permanently affixed to land.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'Real Property' (law.cornell.edu/wex/real_property)

question: An item of personal property that has been attached to real property in such a way that it is legally treated as part of the real property is called a:
explanation: A fixture is an item that was once personal property but has become attached to real property in a manner that classifies it as real property. Fixtures transfer with the real property upon sale unless excluded by agreement.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'Fixture' (law.cornell.edu/wex/fixture)

question: Courts most commonly apply which three tests to determine whether an item has become a fixture?
choice_a: Price paid, color, and brand of the item
choice_b: Weight of the item, date of purchase, and manufacturer's warranty
choice_c: Method of attachment, adaptability to the property's use, and intention of the party who installed it
choice_d: Size of the item, location in the building, and resale value
explanation: The classic tests for determining whether an item is a fixture are the method of attachment (how firmly it is affixed), adaptability (how essential it is to the property's use), and the intention of the person who installed it.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'Fixture' (law.cornell.edu/wex/fixture)

question: A restaurant tenant installs a large walk-in cooler and custom bar built specifically for the tenant's business operations. When the lease ends, these items are known as:
explanation: Trade fixtures are items installed by a commercial tenant for business purposes. Unlike ordinary fixtures, trade fixtures remain the tenant's personal property and may be removed at the end of the lease term, provided the tenant repairs any resulting damage.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'Fixture' (law.cornell.edu/wex/fixture)

question: A farmer sells land but wants to reserve the right to harvest this season's already-planted corn crop after closing. In real property law, annual, cultivated crops like this are classified as:
choice_a: Emblements (fructus industriales), treated as personal property
explanation: Growing crops that require annual cultivation (emblements, or fructus industriales) are generally treated as personal property, distinct from perennial vegetation like trees, which is considered part of the real property.
source_note: Standard real property law doctrine on emblements/fructus industriales; general national real estate licensing curriculum

question: Which legal description method identifies a parcel by tracing its boundary using a point of beginning, compass directions, distances, and monuments, then returning to the point of beginning?
explanation: Metes and bounds describes a parcel's boundaries using courses (compass directions) and distances, along with natural or artificial monuments, tracing the perimeter from a defined point of beginning back to that same point.
source_note: Wikipedia, 'Metes and bounds'

question: In a metes and bounds description, if a natural monument (such as a creek) conflicts with a stated compass bearing and distance, which generally controls?
choice_b: The stated compass bearing always controls
choice_c: The natural monument generally controls, as courts have historically prioritized monuments over courses and distances
explanation: Courts have long established a priority for resolving inconsistencies in metes and bounds descriptions, generally placing natural monuments highest, followed by artificial monuments, then courses (directions), with distances given the least weight.
source_note: Wikipedia, 'Metes and bounds' (priority of calls in boundary resolution)

question: Under the U.S. Public Land Survey System (government rectangular survey), a township is a square parcel measuring approximately:
explanation: Under the government rectangular survey system, a township is a square approximately 6 miles by 6 miles, formed by the intersection of township lines (running east-west) and range lines (running north-south).
source_note: Wikipedia, 'Public Land Survey System'

question: How many sections are contained in one standard township under the government survey system, and how many acres does each section contain?
explanation: A standard township contains 36 sections, numbered in a boustrophedon (back-and-forth) pattern beginning in the northeast corner. Each section is approximately one square mile, or 640 acres.
source_note: Wikipedia, 'Public Land Survey System'

question: A quarter-quarter section under the government rectangular survey system contains approximately how many acres?
explanation: A section (640 acres) divided into quarters yields quarter-sections of 160 acres; dividing a quarter-section into quarters again yields quarter-quarter sections of approximately 40 acres each, the source of the phrase 'the lower 40.'
source_note: Wikipedia, 'Public Land Survey System'

question: Which legal description method is most commonly used for parcels within a recorded subdivision, referencing a map filed in the public land records?
choice_c: Lot, block, and plat (subdivision plat) method
explanation: The lot-and-block (plat) method identifies a specific parcel by its lot number and block number as shown on a subdivision plat map that has been recorded in the county land records, incorporating that map by reference.
source_note: Standard national real estate licensing curriculum on legal description methods; consistent with PLSS/metes-and-bounds material at Wikipedia 'Public Land Survey System'

question: The concept that land ownership traditionally extends upward into the airspace above the surface and downward to the center of the earth is best summarized by which Latin maxim?
choice_d: Cuius est solum, eius est usque ad coelum et ad inferos
explanation: This maxim, roughly translated as 'whoever owns the soil owns up to the sky and down to the depths,' expresses the traditional common-law concept that land ownership includes air rights above and mineral/subsurface rights below the surface, though modern law has limited air rights (e.g., aviation) and subsurface rights can be severed by conveyance.
source_note: Standard national real estate licensing curriculum on air rights and subsurface rights; consistent with real property bundle-of-rights doctrine at Cornell LII Wex 'Real Property'

question: A landowner sells the mineral rights beneath their land to a mining company while retaining ownership of the surface. This is an example of:
choice_a: A severance of subsurface (mineral) rights from surface rights
explanation: Ownership of land can be divided vertically. An owner may sever and separately convey subsurface mineral rights while retaining surface ownership, creating separate legal estates in the same physical location.
source_note: Standard national real estate licensing curriculum on subsurface rights and severance of mineral estates

question: Water rights belonging to an owner of land bordering a flowing waterway such as a river or stream are known as:
explanation: Riparian rights are the rights of a landowner whose property borders a river or stream, including reasonable use of the water for domestic, agricultural, and recreational purposes, subject to the public trust doctrine.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'Riparian rights' (law.cornell.edu/wex/riparian_rights)

question: Water rights belonging to an owner of land bordering a large, non-flowing body of water such as a lake or ocean are generally known as:
explanation: Littoral rights apply to landowners whose property borders a lake, sea, or ocean, as distinguished from riparian rights, which apply to land bordering a flowing waterway such as a river or stream.
source_note: Standard national real estate licensing curriculum distinguishing riparian and littoral rights; consistent with riparian-rights framework at Cornell LII Wex 'Riparian rights'

question: The gradual and imperceptible addition of soil to waterfront land through the natural action of water is called:
explanation: Accretion is the gradual, imperceptible buildup of soil deposited by water action, and the newly formed land generally belongs to the riparian or littoral owner. This differs from avulsion, which is a sudden loss or gain of land, often from a flood or the shifting of a watercourse.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'Riparian rights' (accretion referenced as a riparian entitlement); standard national curriculum for the accretion/erosion/avulsion distinction

question: An unauthorized physical intrusion of a structure, such as a fence or building overhang, onto a neighboring owner's land is called:
explanation: An encroachment is an unauthorized intrusion onto a neighboring property, such as a fence, wall, or building extension that crosses the boundary line. It is typically discovered through a survey and may be resolved by removal, negotiation, sale of the affected strip, or granting an easement.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'Encroachment' (law.cornell.edu/wex/encroachment)

question: Which term describes a nonpossessory right to use another person's land for a specific purpose, such as a shared driveway or utility line?
explanation: An easement is a nonpossessory interest that grants the right to use another's land for a specific purpose without transferring ownership or the right to exclusive possession.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'Easement' (law.cornell.edu/wex/easement)

question: An easement that benefits a particular parcel of land and passes automatically with the transfer of that land, involving both a dominant and a servient tenement, is called an:
explanation: An easement appurtenant benefits a specific parcel of land (the dominant tenement) and burdens another parcel (the servient tenement). It runs with the land, meaning it transfers automatically to subsequent owners of the dominant estate.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'Easement' (law.cornell.edu/wex/easement)

question: In an easement appurtenant, the parcel of land that receives the benefit of the easement is called the:
explanation: The dominant tenement (or dominant estate) is the parcel that benefits from and holds the right to use the easement. The servient tenement is the parcel burdened by allowing that use.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'Easement' (law.cornell.edu/wex/easement)

question: A utility company holds the right to run power lines across many different landowners' properties, without that right being tied to the utility company's ownership of any adjacent parcel. This is an example of:
explanation: An easement in gross benefits a person or entity (such as a utility company) rather than a particular parcel of land, and it does not require a dominant tenement. It is personal to the holder rather than running with adjacent land.
source_note: Standard national real estate licensing curriculum distinguishing easement appurtenant from easement in gross; consistent with dominant/servient framework at Cornell LII Wex 'Easement'

question: An easement created because a landlocked parcel has no other legal access to a public road is known as an easement by:
explanation: An easement by necessity arises when a parcel is landlocked and requires access across a neighboring parcel to reach a public road. Such an easement may terminate if the necessity for it later ceases to exist.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'Easement' (law.cornell.edu/wex/easement)

question: An easement acquired by openly and continuously using another's land without permission for a statutorily defined period is known as an easement by:
explanation: A prescriptive easement arises from open, continuous, and adverse use of another's land for a period of time set by state law, similar in concept to adverse possession but resulting in a use right rather than title.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'Easement' (adverse-possession-based creation referenced); standard national curriculum on prescriptive easements

question: How does a license to use land differ from an easement?
choice_a: A license is permanent and runs with the land, while an easement is temporary
choice_b: A license can only be granted to government entities
choice_c: There is no legal difference between a license and an easement
choice_d: A license is a personal, revocable permission to use land that does not create an interest in the property, while an easement is a nonpossessory property interest
explanation: A license is a personal, generally revocable permission to use land for a specific purpose (such as a ticket to a concert venue). Unlike an easement, a license does not create a property interest and does not run with the land.
source_note: Standard national real estate licensing curriculum distinguishing licenses from easements; consistent with nonpossessory-interest framework at Cornell LII Wex 'Easement'

question: A creditor's legal claim against a property that secures payment of a debt or obligation is known as a:
explanation: A lien is a security interest or legal right acquired by a creditor in a debtor's property, allowing the creditor to prevent sale of the property or seek satisfaction of the debt from it until the obligation is paid.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'Lien' (law.cornell.edu/wex/lien)

question: A lien that attaches to all of a debtor's property, both real and personal, rather than to one specific parcel, is called a:
explanation: A general lien attaches to all of a debtor's property (both real and personal), such as an IRS tax lien or a judgment lien, whereas a specific lien attaches only to a particular, identified piece of property, such as a mortgage or mechanic's lien.
source_note: Standard national real estate licensing curriculum on general vs. specific liens; consistent with lien-security-interest framework at Cornell LII Wex 'Lien'

question: A contractor who has not been paid for labor and materials used to improve a specific property may file which type of lien against that property?
explanation: A mechanic's lien (also called a construction or materialman's lien) is a specific, involuntary lien filed by a contractor, subcontractor, or supplier who has not been paid for labor or materials furnished to improve a particular property.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'Lien' (mechanic's lien listed among specialized lien types)

question: A lien that a property owner voluntarily creates by pledging their property as collateral for a loan, such as when signing a mortgage, is best classified as a:
explanation: A voluntary lien is one the property owner agrees to create, such as a mortgage lien given to a lender as security for a loan. Involuntary liens, by contrast, are imposed by law without the owner's consent, such as tax liens, judgment liens, and mechanic's liens.
source_note: Standard national real estate licensing curriculum on voluntary vs. involuntary liens; consistent with security-interest framework at Cornell LII Wex 'Lien'

question: Which of the following is generally true regarding real property tax liens compared to most other liens against real estate?
choice_a: Property tax liens typically take priority over other liens regardless of when those other liens were recorded
choice_b: Property tax liens are always subordinate to previously recorded mortgage liens
choice_c: Property tax liens are voluntary liens
choice_d: Property tax liens can never be enforced through foreclosure
explanation: Real property tax liens are generally given superior (first) priority over other liens against the property, such as mortgages, regardless of recording date, reflecting the government's strong interest in collecting property taxes.
source_note: Standard national real estate licensing curriculum on lien priority; consistent with statutory-lien category at Cornell LII Wex 'Lien'

question: Restrictions placed on the use of land, liens, easements, and encroachments are all examples of what broad category of interest in real property?
explanation: An encumbrance is any claim, charge, or liability that attaches to real property and may diminish its value or restrict its use, including liens, easements, restrictive covenants, and encroachments. Encumbrances do not necessarily prevent transfer of title.
source_note: Standard national real estate licensing curriculum grouping liens, easements, and encroachments under 'encumbrances'; consistent with lien and easement definitions at Cornell LII Wex

question: The most complete form of ownership interest in real property, granting the owner unlimited duration and full rights of use, possession, and disposition, is called:
explanation: Fee simple absolute is the highest form of ownership recognized in law, granting the owner unlimited duration of ownership along with the full bundle of rights: possession, use, control, exclusion, and disposition.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'Fee simple' (law.cornell.edu/wex/fee_simple)

question: A deed conveys land 'to the City, so long as the land is used as a public park.' If the city stops using the land as a park, ownership automatically reverts to the grantor. This describes a:
explanation: A fee simple determinable automatically terminates and reverts to the grantor (or the grantor's heirs) upon the occurrence of a stated condition, without the need for any further action by the grantor. Language such as 'so long as' or 'while used for' typically signals this estate.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'Fee simple' (law.cornell.edu/wex/fee_simple)

question: A deed conveys land 'to the City, but if the land is ever used for anything other than a public park, the grantor may re-enter and reclaim the property.' This describes a fee simple:
explanation: A fee simple subject to a condition subsequent gives the grantor the right, but not the automatic result, to retake the property if a stated condition occurs. Unlike a fee simple determinable, title does not revert automatically; the grantor must exercise a right of re-entry.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'Fee simple' (law.cornell.edu/wex/fee_simple)

question: An estate that grants an individual the right to possess and use property only for the duration of their own lifetime, after which the property reverts to the original owner or passes to a named third party, is called a:
explanation: A life estate allows the holder (the life tenant) to possess and use the property for the length of a specified life. Upon that person's death, the property reverts to the grantor (a reversion) or passes to a designated third party (a remainder).
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'Fee simple' (law.cornell.edu/wex/fee_simple)

question: A life estate that is measured by the lifetime of someone other than the life tenant is known as a life estate:
explanation: A life estate 'pur autre vie' (French for 'for the life of another') is measured by the life of a person other than the life tenant. For example, A may be granted a life estate measured by the life of B, ending upon B's death regardless of when A dies.
source_note: Standard national real estate licensing curriculum on life estate variants; consistent with life-estate framework at Cornell LII Wex 'Fee simple'

question: When a life estate ends and the property automatically returns to the original grantor (rather than to a third party), the grantor's future interest is called a:
explanation: A reversion is the future interest retained by a grantor when they convey a lesser estate (such as a life estate) and the property is set to return to the grantor once that lesser estate ends.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'Fee simple' (reversion concept for life estates); standard national curriculum distinguishing reversion from remainder

question: When a life estate is created and the property is set to pass to a named third party (rather than back to the original grantor) upon the life tenant's death, that third party holds a future interest called a:
explanation: A remainder is a future interest held by a third party (the 'remainderman') that becomes possessory automatically when a preceding estate, such as a life estate, ends, without reverting to the original grantor.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'Fee simple' (remainder interests referenced under future interests); standard national curriculum on remainder vs. reversion

question: The term used to describe the collection of legal rights associated with property ownership, including the rights of possession, control, exclusion, enjoyment, and disposition, is:
explanation: The 'bundle of rights' is a foundational concept describing property ownership as a collection of separate legal rights, commonly summarized as the rights to possess, use/control, exclude others, enjoy, and dispose of (sell, lease, will, or otherwise transfer) the property. Any of these rights can be separated from the bundle and conveyed individually (for example, granting an easement transfers a right of use without transferring title).
source_note: Standard national real estate licensing curriculum on the 'bundle of rights' doctrine; consistent with the ownership-rights framework at Cornell LII Wex 'Real Property'

question: When two or more people own real property together, each holding an undivided interest with an automatic right of survivorship, this form of co-ownership is called:
explanation: Joint tenancy is a form of co-ownership in which each owner holds an undivided interest in the whole property, and upon the death of one joint tenant, that owner's interest passes automatically to the surviving joint tenant(s), bypassing probate (the right of survivorship).
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'Joint tenancy' (law.cornell.edu/wex/joint_tenancy)

question: Which four 'unities' are traditionally required to be present at the same time for a valid joint tenancy to be created?
choice_a: Unity of price, location, size, and zoning
choice_b: Unity of marriage, age, citizenship, and residency
choice_c: Unity of deed, mortgage, lien, and lease
choice_d: Unity of time, title, interest, and possession
explanation: The traditional four unities required for a joint tenancy are unity of time (interests acquired at the same time), title (acquired through the same instrument), interest (equal ownership shares), and possession (equal right to possess the whole property). If any unity is broken, the joint tenancy may be severed.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'Joint tenancy' (law.cornell.edu/wex/joint_tenancy)

question: In a joint tenancy, if the deed fails to clearly express the intent to create a joint tenancy with right of survivorship, courts will generally presume the co-owners hold title as:
explanation: Because the unity of title required for joint tenancy requires clear language creating survivorship rights, courts generally favor and default to tenancy in common when a deed's intent is ambiguous, since tenancy in common does not depend on the four unities.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'Joint tenancy' (law.cornell.edu/wex/joint_tenancy)

question: Which form of co-ownership does NOT include a right of survivorship, meaning a deceased owner's share passes through their estate to their heirs or devisees rather than automatically to the co-owners?
choice_d: Community property with right of survivorship
explanation: Tenancy in common allows co-owners to hold separate, undivided interests (which may be unequal) without a right of survivorship. When a tenant in common dies, their interest passes according to their will or the laws of intestate succession, not automatically to the other co-owners.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'Joint tenancy' (contrasted with tenancy in common)

question: A form of co-ownership available only to married couples (or, in many states, registered domestic partners), which includes a right of survivorship and generally cannot be severed by one spouse acting alone, is called:
explanation: Tenancy by the entirety is a special form of co-ownership available only to married couples (and, in some jurisdictions, registered domestic partners) that includes a right of survivorship and generally requires both spouses to act together to convey or encumber the property, offering additional creditor protection.
source_note: Standard national real estate licensing curriculum on tenancy by the entirety, a recognized co-ownership form distinct from joint tenancy and tenancy in common as classified at Cornell LII Wex 'Joint tenancy'

question: When a single individual holds full and exclusive ownership of a property with no co-owners, this is referred to as ownership in:
explanation: Ownership in severalty means the property is owned by a single person or single legal entity (such as one corporation), severed from ownership by anyone else, as opposed to concurrent ownership by two or more parties.
source_note: Standard national real estate licensing curriculum on sole ownership ('severalty'), distinguished from the concurrent-ownership forms at Cornell LII Wex 'Joint tenancy'

question: A nonfreehold (leasehold) estate that has a definite, fixed beginning and ending date agreed to by the landlord and tenant is known as a(n):
explanation: An estate (or tenancy) for years is a leasehold with a specific, agreed-upon start and end date. Despite its name, it can be for any fixed duration, even less than one year, and terminates automatically at the end of the term without notice.
source_note: Standard national real estate licensing curriculum on leasehold estate classifications; general leasehold framework confirmed at Cornell LII Wex 'Leasehold'

question: A leasehold estate that automatically renews for successive equal periods (such as month-to-month or year-to-year) until either party gives proper notice of termination is known as a(n):
explanation: A periodic tenancy continues for successive, equal intervals (for example, month-to-month) and automatically renews unless either the landlord or tenant provides the legally required notice to terminate.
source_note: Standard national real estate licensing curriculum on leasehold estate classifications; general leasehold framework confirmed at Cornell LII Wex 'Leasehold'

question: A tenancy that exists with the landlord's permission but without a fixed term or defined periodic rent-payment schedule, and which either party may terminate on reasonable notice, is a:
explanation: A tenancy at will has no fixed duration and continues only as long as both the landlord and tenant agree; it may be terminated by either party at any time upon reasonable notice, and it also terminates automatically upon the death of either party.
source_note: Standard national real estate licensing curriculum on leasehold estate classifications; general leasehold framework confirmed at Cornell LII Wex 'Leasehold'

question: A tenant who continues to occupy a rental property after the lease term has expired, without the landlord's consent, is said to hold a:
explanation: A tenancy at sufferance arises when a tenant who lawfully entered the property remains ('holds over') after the lease has expired, without the landlord's consent. This is the lowest form of leasehold interest and technically makes the tenant a trespasser, though the landlord can elect to treat the occupancy as a new tenancy.
source_note: Standard national real estate licensing curriculum on leasehold estate classifications; general leasehold framework confirmed at Cornell LII Wex 'Leasehold'

question: Which category of estates in land is characterized by an indefinite duration and ownership rights, such as fee simple and life estates, as opposed to leasehold interests?
explanation: Freehold estates (fee simple and life estates) are ownership interests of indefinite or uncertain duration. Nonfreehold (leasehold) estates, by contrast, involve possession for a fixed or determinable period without ownership of the underlying fee.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'Fee simple' (freehold estates category referenced alongside nonfreehold and concurrent estates)

question: A landlord grants a tenant exclusive possession of real property for a specified period in exchange for rent, but the landlord retains a future interest that will become possessory again when the lease ends. The landlord's retained interest during the lease term is best described as a:
explanation: When a landlord leases property to a tenant, the landlord retains a reversionary interest (the leased fee estate), meaning full possessory rights automatically return to the landlord when the leasehold term ends.
source_note: Standard national real estate licensing curriculum applying the reversion concept to landlord-tenant relationships; consistent with reversion doctrine at Cornell LII Wex 'Fee simple'

question: A survey reveals that a neighbor's driveway has been paved 3 feet over the boundary line onto the adjoining owner's lot for the past 25 years, openly and continuously, without the adjoining owner's permission. This scenario is most directly relevant to which two related legal concepts?
choice_c: Encroachment and potential prescriptive easement or adverse possession claim
choice_d: Tenancy by the entirety and community property
explanation: A structure or improvement that physically crosses a boundary line is an encroachment; if the unauthorized use continues openly, continuously, and adversely for the statutory period, it may ripen into a prescriptive easement (a right to continue the use) or, in some circumstances, support an adverse possession claim to the land itself.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'Encroachment' and 'Easement' (prescriptive/adverse-possession-based creation)

question: Which of the following is generally considered part of the 'bundle of rights' that can be separately conveyed, leased, or encumbered without transferring full ownership of the property?
choice_d: All of these are individual rights within the bundle that may be separately conveyed
explanation: Because ownership is conceived as a bundle of separate, severable rights, an owner can convey or restrict individual rights, such as the right of possession (via a lease), the right to exclude (via an easement), or enjoyment (via a life estate), without necessarily transferring the entire bundle or full title.
source_note: Standard national real estate licensing curriculum on the 'bundle of rights' doctrine; consistent with ownership-rights framework at Cornell LII Wex 'Real Property'

question: A homeowners' association's recorded restrictions limiting exterior paint colors and prohibiting fences over four feet tall are examples of:
choice_a: Deed restrictions (restrictive covenants), which are a form of encumbrance
explanation: Deed restrictions, also called restrictive covenants, are private limitations on the use of land recorded in the chain of title. Like liens and easements, they are a form of encumbrance because they may limit an owner's use of the property, though they do not prevent the owner from holding or transferring title.
source_note: Standard national real estate licensing curriculum classifying restrictive covenants as encumbrances; consistent with encumbrance framework drawn from Cornell LII Wex 'Lien' and 'Easement'
